title: Strings
summary: A string is a piece of text, such as a name or a sentence. Quote marks show where it starts and ends.
introduction: A string is a piece of text, such as a name or a sentence. Quote marks show where it starts and ends. Join a name to a greeting. Then find a letter, make text lowercase and put a value into a longer sentence.
learningObjectives: Create strings with single, double and triple quotes and escape sequences
Extract characters and substrings with indexing and slicing
Transform text with methods such as strip(), split(), join() and replace()
Format values inside f-strings with width, precision and thousands separators

blocks.text: A string literal is text between quotes. Single and double quotes are equivalent; pick the one that lets you avoid escaping the other inside the text. Triple quotes (`"""` or `'''`) create strings that span several lines, which is also how docstrings are written.

blocks.title: quotes.py
blocks.code:
single = 'Python'
double = "It's a snake"
escaped = "She said \"hi\"\tthen left.\nNew line."
multi = """Roses are red,
violets are blue."""

print(single, double)
print(escaped)
print(multi)
print(len(multi))

blocks.title: python quotes.py
blocks.content:
Python It's a snake
She said "hi"	then left.
New line.
Roses are red,
violets are blue.
32

blocks.text: Backslash escapes stand for characters that are awkward to type: `\n` is a new line, `\t` a tab, `\"` a literal quote and `\\` a single backslash. The line break inside the triple-quoted string counts as one character, which is why `len(multi)` is 32. Prefix a literal with `r` (raw) to switch escapes off, which is handy for Windows paths and regular expressions: `r"C:\Users\ada"`.

A string is a sequence, so every character has a position, counting from `0`. Negative indexes count from the end: `-1` is the last character. A **slice** `text[start:stop]` returns the characters from `start` up to but *not including* `stop`; leaving either side empty means from the beginning or to the end, and a third number sets the step.

blocks.title: slicing.py
blocks.code:
word = "Python"

print(word[0], word[-1])
print(word[0:3])
print(word[3:])
print(word[:2])
print(word[::2])
print(word[::-1])
print(len(word), "P" in word, "x" in word)

blocks.title: python slicing.py
blocks.content:
P n
Pyt
hon
Py
Pto
nohtyP
6 True False

blocks.text: `word[::2]` takes every second character and `word[::-1]` walks backwards, the shortest way to reverse a string. Slices never fail on out-of-range positions (`word[2:100]` is simply `"thon"`), but a single index outside the string raises `IndexError`.
Strings cannot be changed in place

Strings are **immutable**: once created, their characters never change. Trying to assign to a position fails, which is good news for correctness (no function can quietly alter the text you passed in) but means every transformation produces a *new* string.

blocks.title: python immutable.py
blocks.content:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/ada/projects/immutable.py", line 2, in <module>
    word[0] = "J"
    ~~~~^^^
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

blocks.title: Methods return new strings
blocks.text: Because strings are immutable, `name.upper()` on its own line does nothing visible: it builds an upper-case copy and throws it away. Assign the result (`name = name.upper()`) or use it directly in an expression. The same applies to `strip()`, `replace()` and every other string method.
Methods are called with a dot on the value, and because each returns a new string you can chain them: `title.strip().title()` strips first, then capitalises each word.

blocks.title: methods.py
blocks.code:
title = "  the python tutorial  "

print(title.strip())
print(title.strip().title())
print(title.upper().strip())
print("python".capitalize(), "PYTHON".lower())
print(title.replace("python", "SQL").strip())
print(title.strip().startswith("the"), "tutorial" in title)
print(title.find("python"), title.count("t"))

blocks.title: python methods.py
blocks.content:
the python tutorial
The Python Tutorial
THE PYTHON TUTORIAL
Python python
the SQL tutorial
True True
6 4

rows: Remove whitespace (or the characters you pass) from both ends, the left or the right
Change case; `title()` capitalises every word, `capitalize()` only the first
Return a copy with every occurrence of `old` replaced by `new`
Test the beginning or the end; the `in` operator tests anywhere
Index of the first match, or `-1` if absent; `index(x)` raises `ValueError` instead
Test what kind of characters the string holds, for example before converting user input

blocks.text: `split()` cuts a string into a list of pieces: with no argument it splits on any run of whitespace, otherwise on the separator you give. `join()` is its mirror image, and it is called on the *separator*, which surprises everyone once: `", ".join(items)`.

blocks.title: split_join.py
blocks.code:
sentence = "learn python one step at a time"
words = sentence.split()
print(words)
print(len(words))

csv_line = "Ada,36,London"
name, age, city = csv_line.split(",")
print(name, age, city)

print(" - ".join(words))
print("".join(reversed(name)))

blocks.title: python split_join.py
blocks.content:
['learn', 'python', 'one', 'step', 'at', 'a', 'time']
7
Ada 36 London
learn - python - one - step - at - a - time
adA

blocks.text: `name, age, city = csv_line.split(",")` unpacks the three pieces into three variables in one statement; it fails with `ValueError` if the number of pieces does not match, which is usually what you want with structured input.

An **f-string** is a literal prefixed with `f` in which any expression inside curly braces is evaluated and inserted. After the expression, a colon introduces a *format specification*: how many decimals, how wide, which alignment, whether to add thousands separators. Since Python 3.12 the expression may even contain the same kind of quotes as the string around it.

blocks.title: fstrings.py
blocks.code:
item = "notebook"
price = 4.5
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity

print(f"{quantity} x {item} = {total}")
print(f"Total: {total:.2f} EUR")
print(f"{item:>12}|{price:<8}|")
print(f"{1234567.891:,.1f}")
print(f"{0.256:.1%}")
print(f"{item!r} has {len(item)} letters")
print(f"{"-" * 20}")

blocks.title: Older formatting styles
blocks.text: You will meet `"{} is {}".format(name, age)` and `"%s is %d" % (name, age)` in older code. Both still work, but f-strings are shorter, faster and easier to read, so use them in new code.

questions.question: What does `"Python"[1:4]` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: A slice starts at the first index and stops *before* the second: positions 1, 2 and 3 are `y`, `t` and `h`.

questions.question: Calling `text.upper()` converts the variable `text` to upper case in place.
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable. `upper()` returns a new string; `text` keeps its old value unless you assign the result back to it.
